title: Sēf's cousin is getting married
goal: Hear Sēf's wedding news, congratulate him, accept the invitation and answer ʿugbālak
tip: Wedding plans use the future b-: biyitzawwaj 'he's getting married', biykūnūn hnāk 'they'll be there'. When a wedding comes up, people tell an unmarried friend ʿugbālak 'may you be next'. The fixed reply is allāh yismaʿ minnak 'from your lips to God's ears'.
dialogue: A
عندي لك خبر: ولد عمي حمد بيتزوج!
ʿindi lak khabar: wild ʿammi Ḥamad biyitzawwaj!
I've got news for you: my cousin Ḥamad is getting married!
B
صج؟ مبروك! متى العرس؟
ṣij? mabrūk! mita l-ʿirs?
Really? Congratulations! When's the wedding?
A
الله يبارك فيك. الأسبوع الياي، وانت معزوم
allāh ybārik fīk. il-usbūʿ il-yāy, w inta maʿzūm
Thank you. Next week, and you're invited.
B
أنا؟ بس ما أعرف المعرس زين
ana? bas ma aʿarf il-miʿris zēn
Me? But I don't really know the groom.
A
عادي، كل الشباب بيكونون هناك
ʿādi, kill ish-shabāb biykūnūn hnāk
That's fine, all the guys will be there.
B
زين، بروح وياك. شو ألبس؟
zēn, barūḥ wiyyāk. shu albas?
OK, I'll go with you. What shall I wear?
A
البس كندورة. وعقبالك يا سالم!
ilbas kandūra. w ʿugbālak yā Sālim!
Wear a kandura. And may you be next, Sālim!
B
الله يسمع منك! بس أنا للحين طالب
allāh yismaʿ minnak! bas ana lil-ḥīn ṭālib
From your lips to God's ears! But I'm still a student.
items: he's getting married, he'll get married
she's getting married: bititzawwaj (بتتزوج); married (a man): mitzawwij (you know it)
a woman: maʿzūma (معزومة); a group: maʿzūmīn (معزومين)
biykūn = he'll be, it'll be (you know it)
may you be next (to a man; said to someone unmarried at a wedding)
to a woman: ʿugbālich (عقبالج); also said at graduations; the reply: allāh yismaʿ minnak
from your lips to God's ears (reply to ʿugbālak) (to a man)
to a woman: allāh yismaʿ minnich (الله يسمع منج)
culture: The white robe Emirati men wear is the kandūra; in Kuwait it is usually called the dishdāsha. At his wedding an Emirati groom traditionally wears a white kandūra with a black bisht, a light cloak worn over it for special occasions.

title: At Ḥamad's wedding
goal: In the men's hall at Ḥamad's wedding, congratulate the groom's father, praise the groom and leave with bil-afrāḥ dāymīn
tip: Wishes to a whole family take group endings: mabrūk ʿalēkum 'congratulations to you all', bil-afrāḥ dāymīn 'may you always have happy occasions' (dāymīn is plural). Answer a good wish with w inta baʿad 'you too'; to a group, w intu baʿad.
grammar: recycle: group endings in wishes (mabrūk ʿalēkum, dāymīn)
dialogue: B
السلام عليكم يا عمي. مبروك عليكم!
as-salāmu ʿalaykum yā ʿammi. mabrūk ʿalēkum!
Hello, sir. Congratulations to you all!
A
وعليكم السلام. الله يبارك فيك، حياك الله
wa ʿalaykum is-salām. allāh ybārik fīk, ḥayyāk allāh
Hello. Thank you, welcome.
B
الله يحييك. أنا سالم، ربيع سيف
allāh yḥayyīk. ana Sālim, rbīʿ Sēf
Thank you. I'm Sālim, Sēf's friend.
A
تفضل يا ولدي، اقعد هني
tfaẓẓal yā wildi, igʿid hni
Come in, son, sit here.
B
ما شاء الله، القاعة مليانة!
mā shāʼ allāh, il-gāʿa malyāna!
Mā shāʼ allāh, the hall's full!
A
هيه، كل الرياييل هني، والحريم في القاعة الثانية
hē, kill ir-ryāyīl hni, w il-ḥarīm fi l-gāʿa th-thānya
Yes, all the men are here, and the women are in the other hall.
B
المعرس كشخة! يلا، بالأفراح دايمين
il-miʿris kashkha! yalla, bil-afrāḥ dāymīn
(Later) The groom looks great! Well, may you always have happy occasions.
A
وانت بعد، إن شاء الله. نشوفك في عرسك!
w inta baʿad, in shāʼ allāh. nshūfak fi ʿirsak!
You too, God willing. See you at your own wedding!
items: congratulations (to a family or a group)
to one man: mabrūk ʿalēk (مبروك عليك); the reply is still allāh ybārik fīk
to a woman: igʿidi hni (اقعدي هني); to a group: igʿdu hni
the hall (for a wedding or a party)
full (a feminine thing: a hall, a room)
looking great, smart, stylish (at weddings, Eid)
may you always have happy occasions (to a family; at weddings and Eid)
the reply: w inta baʿad (وانت بعد)
you too, the same to you (to a man)
to a woman: w inti baʿad (وانتي بعد); to a group: w intu baʿad (وانتو بعد)
to a woman: fi ʿirsich (في عرسج)
culture: At an Emirati wedding, men and women celebrate apart, often in two halls next to each other. The men's party is the simpler one, often with traditional cane line dancing. Before the big day, the marriage contract is signed in front of male witnesses at a small ceremony called the milcha, and the bride's female friends hold a henna party for her.

title: Sēf's sister has had a boy
goal: Congratulate Sēf on his new nephew with mabrūk and mā shāʼ allāh, and ask the baby's name
tip: Gulf Arabic says a mother 'brought' her baby: yābat wild 'she had a boy', yābat bint 'she had a girl'. sammaw 'they named' takes object endings: sammōh 'they named him', sammōha 'they named her'. For a newborn, say mabrūk and then mā shāʼ allāh.
grammar: recycle: past tense with object endings (yābat, sammōh)
dialogue: A
أبشرك، أختي يابت ولد!
abashshrak, ukhti yābat wild!
Good news: my sister's had a baby boy!
B
مبروك! ما شاء الله. شو سموه؟
mabrūk! mā shāʼ allāh. shu sammōh?
Congratulations! Mā shāʼ allāh. What have they called him?
A
الله يبارك فيك. سموه محمد، على اسم أبوي
allāh ybārik fīk. sammōh Muḥammad, ʿala ism ubūy
Thank you. They've called him Muḥammad, after my dad.
B
حلو! يعني انت الحين خال!
ḥilu! yaʿni inta l-ḥīn khāl!
Lovely! So you're an uncle now!
A
هيه! وأمي مستانسة وايد، هذا أول حفيد
hē! w ummi mistānsa wāyid, hādha awwal ḥafīd
Yes! And my mum's so happy: he's the first grandchild.
B
ما شاء الله! والبيبي يشبه منو؟
mā shāʼ allāh! w il-bēbi yishbah minu?
Mā shāʼ allāh! And who does the baby look like?
A
الكل يقول إنه يشبه أبوه. شوف الصورة
il-kill ygūl innah yishbah ubūh. shūf iṣ-ṣūra
Everyone says he looks like his dad. Look at the photo.
B
ما شاء الله، الله يخليه لكم
mā shāʼ allāh, allāh ykhallīh lakum
Mā shāʼ allāh. God bless him for you all.
items: she's had a baby boy (lit. she brought a boy)
for a girl: shu sammōha? (شو سموها؟)
ʿala ism + a name = named after
your father's brother: ʿamm (you know ʿammi)
he looks like his dad, he takes after his dad
she looks like her mum: tishbah ummha (تشبه أمها)
God bless him for you (said of a child to the family)
of a girl: allāh ykhallīha lakum (الله يخليها لكم)
culture: For a new baby, Gulf people say mabrūk and then add mā shāʼ allāh, the same pair they use for new clothes or a new bag. mā shāʼ allāh praises something while asking God to keep it safe from envy and the evil eye.

title: Are you upset with me?
goal: Notice Sēf has gone quiet, ask if he's upset with you, apologise for sharing his photo and make up
tip: Ask with the past: ziʿalt minni? 'are you upset with me?' (lit. did you get upset with me?); to a woman, ziʿalti minni?. min + ending names the person: minni 'with me', minnah 'with him'. A real apology says what you meant: ma kān gaṣdi 'I didn't mean it', il-ghalaṭ minni 'it's my fault'.
grammar: recycle: past tense with min + ending (ziʿalt minni, il-ghalaṭ minni)
dialogue: B
سيف، شفيك ساكت؟ زعلت مني؟
Sēf, shfīk sākit? ziʿalt minni?
Sēf, why so quiet? Are you upset with me?
A
شوي. ليش طرشت صورتي في القروب؟
shwayy. lēsh ṭarrasht ṣūrti fi l-grūb?
A bit. Why did you send my photo to the group?
B
والله ما كان قصدي. الصورة حلوة!
wallāh ma kān gaṣdi. iṣ-ṣūra ḥilwa!
Honestly, I didn't mean it. It's a nice photo!
A
حلوة؟ الكل قاعد يضحك علي!
ḥilwa? il-kill gāʿid yiẓḥak ʿalay!
Nice? Everyone's laughing at me!
B
سامحني، الغلط مني. بمسحها الحين
sāmiḥni, il-ghalaṭ minni. bamsaḥha l-ḥīn
Sorry, it's my fault. I'll delete it now.
A
خلاص، مب زعلان. بس المرة الياية اسألني أول
khalāṣ, mub zaʿlān. bas il-marra l-yāya isʼalni awwal
OK, I'm not upset. But next time ask me first.
B
أكيد. يعني ما زعلت مني؟
akīd. yaʿni ma ziʿalt minni?
Of course. So you're not cross with me?
A
لا، ما زعلت. يلا، الكرك علي
la, ma ziʿalt. yalla, il-karak ʿalay
No, I'm not. Come on, the karak's on me.
items: are you upset with me? (to a man; lit. did you get upset with me?)
to a woman: ziʿalti minni? (زعلتي مني؟)
I'm not upset (lit. I didn't get upset); you're not upset (to a man)
to a woman: ma ziʿalti (ما زعلتي)
why so quiet? what's up? (to a man)
to a woman: shfīch sākta? (شفيج ساكتة؟)
I didn't mean it, it wasn't on purpose
also: mub gaṣdi (مب قصدي) = that's not what I meant
it's my fault, the mistake's mine
you know ghalṭati (غلطتي), which says the same
I'll delete it (f.), I'll wipe it (f.)
to a woman: isʼalīni awwal (اسأليني أول)
they're laughing at me: yiẓḥakūn ʿalay (يضحكون علي)

title: Sorry, Maryam
goal: Apologise properly to Maryam at the office for not sending her a file: own the mistake and promise it won't happen again
tip: A proper apology owns the mistake. To a woman: abi aʿtadhir minnich 'I'd like to apologise', sāmḥīni 'forgive me'. kint + b- says what you meant to do: kint baṭarrshah 'I was going to send it'. Finish with ma bititkarrar 'it won't happen again'.
grammar: recycle: kint + b- 'was going to'; -ich endings (sāmḥīni, minnich)
dialogue: B
مريم، أبي أعتذر منج. نسيت أطرش لج الملف
Maryam, abi aʿtadhir minnich. nisēt aṭarrish-lich il-malaff
Maryam, I'd like to apologise. I forgot to send you the file.
A
هيه، قعدت أترياه لين المغرب
hē, gaʿadt atrayyāh lēn il-maghrib
Yes, I waited for it until sunset.
B
سامحيني. كنت بطرشه، بس نسيت. الغلط مني
sāmḥīni. kint baṭarrshah, bas nisēt. il-ghalaṭ minni
Sorry. I was going to send it, but I forgot. It's my fault.
A
ما عليه، كلنا نغلط. بس المدير سأل عنه
ma ʿalēh, killna nighlaṭ. bas il-mudīr saʼal ʿannah
Never mind, we all make mistakes. But the manager asked about it.
B
بكلمه وبقول له إن الغلط مني
bakallmah w bagūl-lah inn il-ghalaṭ minni
I'll talk to him and tell him it was my fault.
A
لا تحاتي، أنا كلمته. بس طرشه الحين
la tḥāti, ana kallamtah. bas ṭarrshah il-ḥīn
Don't worry, I've talked to him. But send it now.
B
زين، بطرشه الحين. وإن شاء الله ما بتتكرر
zēn, baṭarrshah il-ḥīn. w in shāʼ allāh ma bititkarrar
OK, I'll send it now. And God willing, it won't happen again.
A
ولا يهمك. وزين إنك قلت لي بنفسك
wala yhimmak. w zēn innak gilt-li b-nafsak
Don't worry about it. And it's good that you told me yourself.
items: I'd like to apologise (to you) (to a woman)
to a man: abi aʿtadhir minnak (أبي أعتذر منك)
I forgot to send you (to a woman)
to a man: nisēt aṭarrish-lak (نسيت أطرش لك)
forgive me, I'm sorry (to a woman)
to a man: sāmiḥni (you know it); to a group: sāmḥūni
I was going to send it (m.)
a feminine thing: kint baṭarrish-ha (كنت بطرشها)
he asked about it (m.), he asked after him
you know asʼal ʿannah 'I'm asking after him'
often with in shāʼ allāh: in shāʼ allāh ma bititkarrar

title: Sēf and Fahad fall out
goal: Help Sēf sort out a misunderstanding with Fahad over a message, and hear how they made up
tip: To sort out a misunderstanding, say what was meant and what was understood: gaṣdak innak mashghūl? 'you meant you were busy?', ʿala bālah inni ma abīh 'he thought I didn't want him'. Give advice with idha + the future: idha huwa rbīʿak, biyifham 'if he's your friend, he'll understand'.
grammar: recycle: reported speech (gaṣdak innak, ʿala bālah inni) and idha + future
dialogue: A
فهد زعلان مني، وما يرد علي
Fahad zaʿlān minni, w ma yrudd ʿalay
Fahad's upset with me, and he won't answer me.
B
أفا! ليش؟ شو صار بينكم؟
afa! lēsh? shu ṣār bēnkum?
Oh no! Why? What happened between you?
A
طرشت له: مب فاضي لك. وفهمني غلط
ṭarrasht-lah: mub fāẓi lak. w fhimni ghalaṭ
I texted him: I'm not free for you. And he got me wrong.
B
قصدك إنك مشغول؟
gaṣdak innak mashghūl?
You meant you were busy?
A
هيه! بس على باله إني ما أبيه
hē! bas ʿala bālah inni ma abīh
Yes! But he thought I didn't want him (around).
B
عيل دق عليه واشرح له. إذا هو ربيعك صج، بيفهم
ʿayal digg ʿalēh w ishraḥ-lah. idha huwa rbīʿak ṣij, biyifham
Then call him and explain. If he's really your friend, he'll understand.
A
كلمته وتصالحنا! ويبينا نزوره في الكويت
kallamtah w tṣālaḥna! w yabīna nzūrah fi l-Kwēt
(The next day) I talked to him and we made up! And he wants us to visit him in Kuwait.
B
زين سويت! متى بنروح؟
zēn sawwēt! mita binrūḥ?
Good for you! When are we going?
items: he won't answer me, he isn't answering me
she won't: ma trudd ʿalay (ما ترد علي)
you mean, you meant (to a man)
to a woman: gaṣdich (قصدج); gaṣdi = I mean
you know ʿala bāli innak 'I thought you'
I talked to him, I called him
you talked to him (to a man): kallamtah too
we made up, we sorted it out
yabīna nzūrah = he wants us to visit him; you know yabīk 'he wants you'

title: Landing in Kuwait
goal: Arrive in Kuwait with Sēf: answer Fahad's Kuwaiti welcome (shlōnkum, nawwartu) and catch his shgilt and inṭirūni
tip: Fahad greets you both with shlōnkum? (UAE shḥālkum?); answer zēnīn il-ḥamdu lillāh. nawwartu 'welcome' (lit. you've brought light) gets in-nūr nūrak. He also says shgilt? for shu gilt? 'what did you say?' and inṭirni 'wait for me' (UAE trayyāni).
grammar: Kuwaiti forms II: shlōnkum, shgilt, inṭirni; recycle mū
dialogue: B
هلا والله فهد!
hala wallāh Fahad!
Hi, Fahad!
A
يا هلا! الحمد لله على سلامتكم. شلونكم؟
yā hala! il-ḥamdu lillāh ʿala salāmatkum. shlōnkum?
Welcome! Thank God you got here safely. How are you both?
B
الله يسلمك. زينين الحمد لله، وانت شحالك؟
allāh ysallmak. zēnīn il-ḥamdu lillāh, w inta shḥālak?
Thank you. We're fine, thank God. And how are you?
A
بخير. نورتوا الكويت!
b-khēr. nawwartu l-Kwēt!
Fine. Welcome to Kuwait!
B
النور نورك. البيت بعيد عن المطار؟
in-nūr nūrak. il-bēt baʿīd ʿan il-maṭār?
Thank you. Is the house far from the airport?
A
شقلت؟ ما سمعتك، المطار زحمة!
shgilt? ma simaʿtak, il-maṭār zaḥma!
What did you say? I didn't hear you, the airport's packed!
B
قلت: البيت بعيد؟
gilt: il-bēt baʿīd?
I said: is the house far?
A
لا، مو بعيد. انطروني هني دقيقة
la, mū baʿīd. inṭirūni hni dagīga
No, it's not far. Wait for me here a minute.
items: warmer than hala (you know it); yā hala wallāh = a big welcome
UAE: shḥālkum? (شحالكم؟); the answer: zēnīn il-ḥamdu lillāh
one person says: zēn il-ḥamdu lillāh
welcome! (lit. you've brought light) (to a group)
to a man: nawwart (نورت); to a woman: nawwarti (نورتي); the reply: in-nūr nūrak
thank you (reply to nawwart; lit. the light is yours) (to a man)
to a woman: in-nūr nūrich (النور نورج); to a group: in-nūr nūrkum (النور نوركم)
what did you say? (to a man) (Kuwait)
to a woman: shgiltī? (شقلتي؟); UAE: shu gilt? (شو قلت؟)
I didn't hear you (to a man)
to a woman: ma simaʿtich (ما سمعتج)
to a woman: inṭiri (انطري); to a group: inṭirūni (انطروني); UAE: trayyāni (ترياني)

title: Meeting Nūra
goal: At Fahad's family home, with Fahad there, meet his sister Nūra: answer her welcome and ask after their mother
tip: Nūra speaks Kuwaiti (ēh, shinu, yumma); you answer in your own Arabic. Replies to a woman take her endings: allāh yḥayyīch, shu giltī?, law samaḥti. A family answers tsharrafna with ish-sharaf lana 'the honour is ours', and il-bēt bētkum means 'make yourselves at home'.
grammar: Kuwaiti forms II: recycle ēh, shinu, yumma; replies to a woman (allāh yḥayyīch, giltī)
dialogue: A
السلام عليكم، حياكم الله. أنا نورة، أخت فهد
as-salāmu ʿalaykum, ḥayyākum allāh. ana Nūra, ukht Fahad
Hello, welcome. I'm Nūra, Fahad's sister.
B
وعليكم السلام. الله يحييج، تشرفنا
wa ʿalaykum is-salām. allāh yḥayyīch, tsharrafna
Hello. Thank you, nice to meet you.
A
الشرف لنا. يمه تسلم عليكم، وتقول البيت بيتكم
ish-sharaf lana. yumma tsallim ʿalēkum, w tgūl il-bēt bētkum
The honour's ours. Mum says hello, and says make yourselves at home.
B
الله يسلمها. والوالدة بخير إن شاء الله؟
allāh ysallimha. w il-wālda b-khēr in shāʼ allāh?
God keep her. I hope your mother's well?
A
إيه، الحمد لله. شنو تشربون؟ قهوة ولّا شاي؟
ēh, il-ḥamdu lillāh. shinu tishrabūn? gahwa walla chāy?
Yes, thank God. What will you have to drink? Coffee or tea?
B
سامحيني، شو قلتي؟
sāmḥīni, shu giltī?
Sorry, what did you say?
A
قهوة ولّا شاي؟ فهد يقول إنك تحب الكرك
gahwa walla chāy? Fahad ygūl innak tḥibb il-karak
Coffee or tea? Fahad says you like karak.
B
هيه، كرك لو سمحتي
hē, karak law samaḥti
Yes, karak, please.
items: to a man: allāh yḥayyīk (you know it); to a group: allāh yḥayyīkum (الله يحييكم)
the honour is ours (reply to tsharrafna, from a family or group)
one person says: ish-sharaf li (you know it)
he says hello: ysallim ʿalēkum (يسلم عليكم); the reply: allāh ysallimha
make yourselves at home (lit. the house is your house) (to a group)
to a man: il-bēt bētak (you know it)
you drink; will you have (a drink)? (to a group)
to a man: tishrab (تشرب); to a woman: tishrabīn (تشربين)
what did you say? (to a woman)
to a man: shu gilt? (شو قلت؟); Kuwait: shgiltī? (شقلتي؟)
to a man: law samaḥt (you know it)

title: What's the story?
goal: Meet Fahad at a café in Kuwait and find out why he's late: his dad's car broke down
tip: A sālfa is a story or a matter: shu s-sālfa? 'what's going on?', sālfa ṭawīla 'it's a long story'. Fahad says shinu s-sālfa? and takfa 'please, I'm begging you' (UAE allāh ykhallīk). Telling a group not to do something takes -ūn: la tgūlūn-lah 'don't tell him'.
grammar: Kuwaiti forms II: shinu s-sālfa, takfa; recycle la + -ūn (la tgūlūn-lah)
dialogue: A
هلا! شنو السالفة؟ وين سيف؟
hala! shinu s-sālfa? wēn Sēf?
Hi! What's going on? Where's Sēf?
B
هلا فيك. راح يصلي. وانت شو السالفة؟ تأخرت!
hala fīk. rāḥ yṣalli. w inta shu s-sālfa? taʼakhkhart!
Hi. He's gone to pray. And what's the story with you? You're late!
A
سالفة طويلة! السيارة خربت في الطريق
sālfa ṭawīla! is-sayyāra khirbat fi ṭ-ṭarīg
Long story! The car broke down on the way.
B
أفا! وانت بخير؟
afa! w inta b-khēr?
Oh no! Are you OK?
A
إيه، الحمد لله. السيارة اللحين في الكراج، بس حق أبوي!
ēh, il-ḥamdu lillāh. is-sayyāra illaḥīn fi l-karāj, bas ḥagg ubūy!
Yes, thank God. The car's at the garage now, but it's my dad's!
B
وشو قال أبوك؟
w shu gāl ubūk?
And what did your dad say?
A
للحين ما يدري. تكفى، لا تقولون له!
lil-ḥīn ma yadri. takfa, la tgūlūn-lah!
He doesn't know yet. Please, I'm begging you, don't tell him!
B
لا تحاتي، ما بنقول شي. بس قول له انت
la tḥāti, ma bingūl shay. bas gūl-lah inta
Don't worry, we won't say a thing. But you tell him yourself.
items: what's going on? what's the story?
fast speech: shsālfa? (you'll see written شسالفة؟); Kuwait: shinu s-sālfa? (شنو السالفة؟)
what's going on? what's the story? (Kuwait)
sālfa = a story, a matter; sawālif (سوالف) = chats, stories
Saudis say it too; UAE: allāh ykhallīk (الله يخليك)
I won't say a thing: ma bagūl shay (ما بقول شي)
she's gone to pray: rāḥat tṣalli (راحت تصلي)

title: Two and a half dinars
goal: Buy a perfume for your mum in a Kuwaiti shop, with Fahad asking the prices in dinars and haggling for you
tip: Kuwait's money is the dīnār. Count it like dirhams: dīnārēn 'two dinars', khams danānīr 'five dinars' (three to ten take the plural), ʿishrīn dīnār from eleven up. Your comparatives work here too: fī shay arkhaṣ? 'is there anything cheaper?', rīḥtah aḥla 'it smells nicer'.
grammar: recycle: numbers with nouns (dīnārēn, khams danānīr) and comparatives (arkhaṣ, aḥla)
dialogue: B
فهد، اسأله: هذا العطر بكم؟
Fahad, isʼalah: hādha l-ʿiṭir b-cham?
Fahad, ask him: how much is this perfume?
A
يقول بخمس دنانير. حيل غالي!
ygūl b-khams danānīr. ḥēl ghāli!
He says five dinars. That's really expensive!
B
صج؟ عيل في شي أرخص؟
ṣij? ʿayal fī shay arkhaṣ?
Really? Is there anything cheaper, then?
A
هذا بدينارين ونص، وريحته أحلى
hādha b-dīnārēn w nuṣṣ, w rīḥtah aḥla
This one's two and a half dinars, and it smells nicer.
B
زين، باخذه. هدية حق أمي
zēn, bākhdhah. hadiyya ḥagg ummi
OK, I'll take it. It's a present for my mum.
A
خله بدينارين، تكفى!
khallah b-dīnārēn, takfa!
(to the shopkeeper) Make it two dinars, please!
B
شو قال لك؟
shu gāl-lak?
What did he say to you?
A
قال زين، بدينارين. عطه الفلوس
gāl zēn, b-dīnārēn. ʿaṭah il-flūs
He said OK, two dinars. Give him the money.
items: a dinar (Kuwait's money); dinars (after eleven and up)
ʿishrīn dīnār = twenty dinars; you know dirham (درهم)
b-dīnārēn w nuṣṣ = two and a half dinars
it smells nicer (lit. its smell is nicer)
a feminine thing: rīḥat-ha aḥla (ريحتها أحلى)
make it two dinars (haggling) (to a man)
to a woman: khallīh b-dīnārēn (خليه بدينارين); in the UAE: khallah b- + a price in dirhams
to a woman: ʿaṭīh (عطيه); you know ʿaṭni 'give me'
culture: Kuwait's money is the Kuwaiti dinar. By law it is divided into a thousand fils.

title: An evening at the diwaniya
goal: Go with Fahad to his father's diwaniya: greet Bū Fahad respectfully, pass on your family's greetings and take his coffee
tip: Bū Fahad means 'Fahad's father'. Greet him first, with respect: yā ʿammi, ṭāl ʿumrak. Agree to a request with ḥāẓir 'certainly'. Pass on your family's greetings with the plural: ysallmūn ʿalēk 'they send their regards'; the reply is allāh ysallimhum 'God keep them'.
grammar: Kuwaiti forms II: id-dīwāniyya, shlōn il-ahal; recycle respectful address (yā ʿammi, ṭāl ʿumrak)
dialogue: B
السلام عليكم يا عمي
as-salāmu ʿalaykum yā ʿammi
Hello, sir.
A
وعليكم السلام. حياك الله يا ولدي، تفضل
wa ʿalaykum is-salām. ḥayyāk allāh yā wildi, tfaẓẓal
Hello. Welcome, son, come in.
B
الله يحييك. ما شاء الله، الديوانية مليانة!
allāh yḥayyīk. mā shāʼ allāh, id-dīwāniyya malyāna!
Thank you. Mā shāʼ allāh, the diwaniya's full!
A
إيه، كل ليلة نقعد هني ونسولف. اقعد يمي
ēh, kill lēla nigʿid hni w nsōlif. igʿid yammi
Yes, every night we sit here and chat. Sit next to me.
B
حاضر طال عمرك. هذي أول مرة أشوف ديوانية
ḥāẓir ṭāl ʿumrak. hādhi awwal marra ashūf dīwāniyya
Certainly, sir. This is the first time I've seen a diwaniya.
A
صج؟ عيل تعال أي وقت. شلون الأهل؟
ṣij? ʿayal taʿāl ay wagt. shlōn il-ahal?
Really? Then come any time. How's your family?
B
بخير الحمد لله، يسلمون عليك
b-khēr il-ḥamdu lillāh, ysallmūn ʿalēk
Fine, thank God. They send their regards.
A
الله يسلمهم. تفضل القهوة يا ولدي
allāh ysallimhum. tfaẓẓal il-gahwa yā wildi
God keep them. Have some coffee, son.
items: the diwaniya (a Kuwaiti men's sitting room and evening gathering) (Kuwait)
a diwaniya: dīwāniyya (ديوانية); plural: duwāwīn (دواوين); in the UAE: il-majlis (you know it)
certainly, right away (agreeing to a request)
to a woman: taʿāli ay wagt (تعالي أي وقت); to a group: taʿālu ay wagt (تعالوا أي وقت)
UAE also: shḥāl il-ahal? (you know it)
(they) send their regards, they say hi (to a man)
to a woman: ysallmūn ʿalēch (يسلمون عليج); the reply: allāh ysallimhum
God keep them (reply when people send their regards)
for him: allāh ysallmah (you know it)
have some coffee (offering it, to a man)
culture: A diwaniya is a reception room in or beside a Kuwaiti home where men of all ages meet to talk about family, community matters and the news; young men learn its manners by watching. Some open every evening, others on set days chosen by the host. Gatherings grow at Ramadan, weddings and funerals, and women increasingly hold their own. In 2025 UNESCO listed it as intangible cultural heritage.

title: Goodbye, Kuwait
goal: Thank Fahad and his family as you leave Kuwait, invite them to Dubai and talk about how Kuwaitis speak
tip: Thank a whole family with group endings: mā gaṣṣartu 'you've all been so kind' (reply: mā sawwēna shay), taʿʿabnākum 'we've put you to so much trouble', la tinsūna 'don't forget us'. Fahad waves the thanks away with la tgūl chidhi 'don't say that', and says ma rāḥ for 'won't'.
grammar: Kuwaiti forms II: ma rāḥ + verb, ḥatta iḥna; recycle group endings (mā gaṣṣartu, la tinsūna)
dialogue: B
يلا فهد، ما قصرتوا والله
yalla Fahad, mā gaṣṣartu wallāh
Well, Fahad, you've all been so kind, honestly.
A
ما سوينا شي. البيت بيتكم أي وقت
mā sawwēna shay. il-bēt bētkum ay wagt
It was nothing. You're welcome here any time.
B
تعبناكم وايد هالأسبوع
taʿʿabnākum wāyid hal-usbūʿ
We've put you to so much trouble this week.
A
لا تقول جذي! إحنا استانسنا حيل
la tgūl chidhi! iḥna istānasna ḥēl
Don't say that! We really enjoyed it.
B
وانتو حياكم في دبي. لا تنسونا!
w intu ḥayyākum fi Dbayy. la tinsūna!
And you're all welcome in Dubai. Don't forget us!
A
الله يحييك. ما راح أنساكم! شرايك في الكويت؟
allāh yḥayyīk. ma rāḥ ansākum! shrāyak fi l-Kwēt?
Thank you. I won't forget you! What do you think of Kuwait?
B
برأيي حلوة وايد! بس اللهجة صعبة شوي
b-raʼyi ḥilwa wāyid! bas il-lahja ṣaʿba shwayy
In my opinion it's lovely! But the dialect's a bit hard.
A
صج، حتى إحنا: أهل شرق غير عن أهل قبلة
ṣij, ḥatta iḥna: ahal Sharg ghēr ʿan ahal Jibla
True, even among us: the people of Sharq are different from the people of Jibla.
items: you've all been so kind, thank you for everything (to a group)
to a man: mā gaṣṣart (you know it); to a woman: mā gaṣṣarti; the reply: mā sawwēna shay
we've put you to a lot of trouble (thanking hosts)
UAE also: la tgūl chī (لا تقول جي); to a woman: la tgūlīn chidhi
to a man: la tinsāna (لا تنسانا)
I won't forget you (to a group) (Kuwait)
UAE: ma bansākum (ما بنساكم); you know ma bansa 'I won't forget'
UAE: ḥatta niḥin (حتى نحن); you know ḥatta ana
culture: Kuwaitis can often tell which old quarter of Kuwait City a family comes from, such as Qibla (Jibla), Al-Murqab or Sharq, by the way they speak. One example: the word for 'sugar' is said shekar in Sharq but shakar in Qibla.
